title: The second of two
hookLine: the cave again: the second of two, do not grieve, Allah is with us (9:40)
carry: small, brave, ordinary things in the dark

lines: YOU SINK DOWN TO THE EARTH.
cards: Late in his life, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calls for the march to Tabuk, in the worst of the heat.
Some people find reasons to stay home, and at-Tawbah, verse thirty-eight, asks them: what's wrong with you, that when you're told to go out, you sink down heavily to the earth?
Then the surah tells them a story they all knew, one you heard on this path last year: the cave of Thawr, the night of the hijra, two men hiding while the searchers walked past.
Back to the cave, then, to see who else was in the story.

teach.h: IF YOU DON'T HELP, GOD ALREADY DID.
teach.b: Verse forty, in paraphrase: if you don't help him, God already helped him, when he was driven out, the second of two, when the two were in the cave, and he said to his companion, in Pickthall's words: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us."
Then God sent down His sakina, His calm, on him. On whom? The verse just says him.
Some commentators say the Prophet; others say Abu Bakr, the companion told not to grieve. The Arabic allows both, and commentators still discuss it.

The verse's point, to the people staying home, is sharp: the Prophet doesn't need you. God helped him when he had one friend. But read the hijra in Bukhari, and the two in the cave weren't quite alone.
Abu Bakr's son 'Abdullah came every night after dark, slept near the cave, and slipped back to Mecca before dawn to listen for news.

teach.h: A SON, A SHEPHERD, A DAUGHTER.
teach.b: A shepherd, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra, grazed sheep over their tracks and brought them milk. And Abu Bakr's daughter Asma', packing their food for the journey, found nothing to tie the bag with.
So she tore her waistband in two and used it to tie up the provisions.
She was called dhat an-nitaqayn, she of the two waistbands.

The second of two is a phrase about friendship under pressure. Around the two in the cave were people who did small, brave, ordinary things in the dark: a torn belt, a night's walk, a flock driven over footprints.

how: Muslims retell the night in the cave of Thawr with the story of the hijra, honoring the household of Abu Bakr who helped, and some comfort a frightened friend with the verse's words, la tahzan, inna Allaha ma'ana: do not grieve, God is with us.

o: the two companions hiding in the cave
she of the two waistbands, Asma's nickname
a sash worn by brides in old Mecca

games.q: around the cave — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an names Abu Bakr in 9:40
the verse says only 'his companion'; Muslim tradition identifies him as Abu Bakr.
all commentators agree on who received the sakina
the verse says 'him'; some say the Prophet, others Abu Bakr.
Asma' tore her own waistband in two to tie up the provisions
that is why she was called dhat an-nitaqayn, she of the two waistbands.

games.q: you're Asma', packing food for your father and the Prophet's dangerous journey. there's nothing to tie the bag with. what do you do?
o: tear your waistband in two and use it.
go and borrow a rope from a neighbor.
games.why: she tore her waistband in two and tied up the provisions with it. she was called she of the two waistbands.

practice: Bring to mind someone who stayed with you on a bad night: a hospital hallway, a long drive, a phone call that went past midnight.

Then the people around that night you hardly thanked, the one who brought food, the one who drove, the one who covered for you at work, and hold them one by one. If you pray, you can ask good for each of them by name.

wordCard.voice: Dhat an-nitaqayn, she of the two waistbands: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma', who tore her belt to tie up the Prophet's food for the hijra.

orig.note: Arabic: "the second of two," the Qur'an's phrase for the Prophet in the cave (9:40).

carryVoice: Your line: small, brave, ordinary things in the dark. Quiet help still counts. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 (the hijra: 'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra, Asma' and her waistband)
